     "subtitle": "The crisis of political discourse and the search for a civilizational minimum",
     "screenshot_description": "Host Marin Marić introduces guest Petar Šarić in the Mladi za Domovinu podcast studio.",
     "content": "In the 115th episode of the podcast of the association **Mladi za Domovinu**, host **Marin Marić** opens the question of the quality of political pluralism in Croatia. Although new political parties appear in every election cycle, Marić warns that public discourse is simultaneously becoming increasingly poisoned and lowered to the level of base passions, whereby an agreement on basic common assumptions in the state is lacking.\n\nIn order to define the fundamental civilizational minimums that should exist in Croatian politics regardless of ideological differences, Marić brings in as a guest **Petar Šarić**, a philosopher, sociologist, and doctoral candidate at the Faculty of Arts in Ljubljana, who also serves as president of the World Youth Alliance and the association Atlas Hrvatska. The goal of their conversation is not to invoke unnatural political coalitions or erase worldview differences, but to establish a common framework within which political actors can conduct debates, while keeping fundamental national and social interests unquestionable.",

     "subtitle": "The phenomenon of political contrarianism: Why is it more important to us who is speaking than what is objectively good?",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić explains the importance of holding to objective principles in politics instead of mere contrarianism.",
     "content": "As a starting point for the discussion, host Marin Marić quotes Šarić's column in which the author problematizes the loss of worldview consistency in the age of mass media. Due to information saturation and manipulations by political elites, citizens and politicians increasingly position themselves exclusively in relation to the opposing political camp, without their own authentic ideological substance.\n\nPetar Šarić explains how in the age of political postmodernity, in which grand narratives and ideologies have vanished, people lose their orientation and fall into the trap of **political contrarianism**. This leads to absurd situations in which individuals advocate one thesis one day, and just ten days later defend a diametrically opposed stance, exclusively because that first thesis was supported in the meantime by someone from the opposing political camp.\n\nMarić illustrates this phenomenon with concrete examples from Croatian everyday life, such as the situation in Lika and the attitude toward public figures and local authorities. He points out how for a part of the left, the singer **Thompson** will always represent the moral bottom regardless of what he did or invested, while on the other hand, the right is not immune to such behavior either. As an example, he cites the current city government in Zagreb: even when an objectively good move is made, such as the renovation of the stadium in Kranjčevićeva or the extension of the tram line, a part of the right-wing critics will a priori look for faults just so they do not have to admit that a political opponent has done something useful.\n\nŠarić agrees that such an approach is not productive and emphasizes that when evaluating any political move, the first criterion must be the question: **is this objectively good for the people, their children, and the future?** Only after that can one discuss who the actors implementing it are. He calls for psychological courage and the abandonment of comfortable tribal frameworks in favor of higher, objective values.",

     "subtitle": "Postmodern politics of power and affective polarization in Croatia",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić connects contemporary political contrarianism with the philosophy of Michel Foucault.",
     "content": "Responding to Marić's question of whether the hyperproduction of new political parties in Croatia is a direct consequence of the fact that parties no longer gather around well-rounded ideological principles, but exclusively as a reaction \"against\" someone, Petar Šarić introduces a deeper philosophical perspective.\n\nHe connects this phenomenon with postmodern conceptions of politics, especially with the teaching of the French philosopher **Michel Foucault**, a well-known representative of the theory of the politics of power. According to this understanding, in politics and society there is no objective truth or objective good at all, but only different camps of power that clash with one another in order to impose their own action as the dominant \"truth\".\n\nŠarić warns that today's politics of contrarianism is a direct reflection of such a philosophy. In such a framework, it ceases to be important what is truly useful for society and the people, and the only important thing becomes who said something and how they can be attacked so that one's own camp takes supremacy. Šarić defines such a relativistic approach to reality as inherently left-wing, regardless of whether it is applied in practice by someone who declares themselves as a leftist or a rightist. Host Marin Marić builds on this with the concept of **affective polarization**, a state in which political divisions are no longer based on ideological consistency and reason, but exclusively on emotions and affects toward the opposing side.",

     "subtitle": "Ecology between the biocentrism of the green left and the anthropocentric approach",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić speaks about the importance of an anthropocentric approach to environmental protection and human dignity.",
     "content": "Moving on to concrete topics around which there should be a national consensus, the interlocutors open the issue of environmental protection. Upon Marić's inquiry into how caring for something so universal became an almost exclusive synonym for the green left, Petar Šarić explains that the roots of this process reach back to the 1980s and 1990s, and even earlier to the hippie movement. When generations raised on that rhetoric took over political positions of power, nature conservation – often accompanied by cataclysmic scientific predictions – was successfully branded as the daily-political agenda of the green left.\n\nHowever, Šarić points out a key ontological difference in the way the left and the conservative right view nature. With the green left, **biocentrism** is present – an understanding of the environment as a self-purposeful system, a sort of neo-pagan cult of \"Mother Earth\" or Gaia, where nature is worshiped above man. If man is thrown out of the center of that story, one arrives at dangerous and absurd theses that Šarić calls a manifestation of the **culture of death**: the idea that the number of people on the planet should be reduced because human beings are mere \"carriers of a carbon footprint\".\n\nIn contrast to this, Šarić strongly advocates a healthy **anthropocentric approach** to environmental protection. Such an approach starts from unquestionable human dignity – the inherent value of every human being that cannot be given to them or taken away from them by any state or international organization. From that perspective, nature is not a deity in itself, but a space in which man coexists with the environment, using its blessings without destruction, precisely so that future generations of people might also enjoy them in the fullness of their dignity.",
     "keywords": [

    {
     "subtitle": "Oikophilia, the principle of subsidiarity, and the traps of global regulations",
     "screenshot_description": "Conversation about Roger Scruton's concept of oikophilia and the difference between a local and global approach to ecology.",
     "content": "Looking for a meeting point between ecological awareness and traditional values, Marin Marić mentions the British philosopher **Roger Scruton** and his concept of **oikophilia** – the love of home that simultaneously encompasses people, customs, culture, and the natural environment. Petar Šarić considers that this concept can be a bridge of cooperation, but warns of a key methodological obstacle that today divides the local conservative approach from the global approach of the green left.\n\nScruton's oikophilia is deeply rooted in the principle of **subsidiarity**, a concept also important in the social teaching of the Church, according to which the responsibility for preserving the environment lies primarily with local communities – the people who feel that space as their own home. On the other hand, the mainstream green left tries to solve the problem according to the \"top-down\" (*top-down*) model, through large international institutions and global regulatory measures.\n\nŠarić warns that such global institutions are often subject to the influences of elite circles and multinational corporations. As a vivid example, he cites the theses on the unsustainability of meat consumption due to the carbon footprint of the cattle industry; if such a ban or strict regulation were imposed from a global level, it would directly destroy the livelihood of small, local cattle breeders and farmers.\n\nReflecting on Marić's remark that on the left there are also anarchist movements that oppose corporations, but also that an individual cannot solve the problem of industrial plastic production by recycling independently, Šarić draws a historical parallel with the conflict between **Karl Marx** and the anarchist **Mikhail Bakunin** within the First International. While the anarchists advocated chaotic action from below, the advocates of large international organizations prevailed because they were more efficient in practice. As a solution for the contemporary world, Šarić proposes a paradoxical \"golden mean\" akin to the original motto of the European Union, *United in diversity*: umbrella international bodies should exist in order to define global problems, but their primary task must be the preservation of the autonomy of local actors who have \"their own skin in the game\" (*skin in the game*).",

     "subtitle": "Nuclear energy and the sociology of culturally conditioned fear",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić, from the perspective of the sociology of risk, explains why the public irrationally fears nuclear energy.",
     "content": "As an excellent example of a topic in which ecological sustainability and economic productivity can be reconciled, the interlocutors single out **nuclear energy**. Petar Šarić points out the absurdity of the situation in which the green left systematically ignores or attacks this source of energy. He recalls the protest of the association **Zelena akcija** against the initiatives of the Ministry of Economy related to the development of nuclear energy in Croatia, although it is a clean and sustainable energy that does not produce greenhouse gases nor depend on the burning of fossil fuels.\n\nTo explain why the promise of nuclear energy – which in the mid-20th century was considered a technology that would lift humanity to the stars – was replaced in the public by resistance, Šarić uses the tools of his narrower scientific field: the **sociology of risk**. He explains how human perception of fear is to a vast extent culturally and media-conditioned through films, articles, social networks, and even podcasts.\n\nHe substantiates his thesis with a personal anecdote from childhood, when after watching a documentary with a visualization of a black hole devouring the Earth – prompted also by the media writings at the time about experiments at **CERN** – he was convinced that such a cataclysm was a real threat in his lifetime. Only later did he realize that it was a media-hyperinflated fear. A similar mechanism, he points out in the conversation with Marić, is also visible in everyday banal fears:\n- **Traffic:** People feel an irrational fear of flying by plane because it seems \"magical\" and unnatural to them, while without thinking they drive personal cars around Zagreb every day, which is statistically incomparably more dangerous.\n- **The animal world:** People in our regions are panically afraid of spiders or snakes, while they perceive mosquitoes as merely a minor nuisance, although it is precisely mosquitoes on a global level that are responsible for hundreds of thousands of deaths annually due to the transmission of diseases.\n\nEqually so, concludes Šarić, resistance toward nuclear power plants is often not the result of a rational calculation of risk, but of culturally imposed panic and political contrarianism.",

     "subtitle": "Why is caring for the environment a first-class patriotic issue?",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić summarizes why the preservation of Croatian nature should be at the center of interest of every patriot.",
     "content": "Rounding off the ecological block of the conversation, host Marin Marić asks the guest to directly and concisely explain to the audience – especially those on the right political spectrum – why it is important for a conservative and a patriot to actively care about ecology.\n\nPetar Šarić answers very vividly, appealing to the collective experience of generations grown up in Croatia: memories of playing on clean grass, drinking healthy water directly from the tap, and the taste of homegrown tomatoes from grandma's garden. He emphasizes how today's generation has a moral duty to enable an identical experience for their children and grandchildren.\n\n> \"Let us not destroy what we have, what our ancestors defended with blood and left to us, but let us simply preserve it for future generations. To me, this is not an ideological issue at all, it is simply a common-sense issue.\"\n\nŠarić warns that the Croatian environment must not be sacrificed for abstract global promises of GDP growth or because someone paid well to dump waste in the suburbs of our cities. He concludes how absurd it is for patriots to ignore the protection of their own country just because that topic is loudly advocated in the public space by someone who is unacceptable to them on other ideological issues. Political struggle, he points out, must not be a self-purposeful pleasure in contrarianism, but a means for defending the objective good.",

     "subtitle": "The power of international corporations, crony capitalism, and the need for healthy protectionism",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić speaks about the negative influence of international corporations on the real estate market and the need to protect domestic citizens.",
     "content": "Opening the second major topic around which the left and the right would have to reach a consensus, Petar Šarić singles out a critical attitude toward the operation of large **international corporations**. Although criticism of corporate power is traditionally perceived as the domain of the left and the struggle for workers' rights, Šarić reminds that within conservative thought as well there is a strong criticism of so-called **crony capitalism** (crony capitalism). After the historical ailments of socialism, Croatian society faced the problematic aspects of the Western model in which international bodies and corporations, having enormous capital at their disposal, dictate the labor market and shape the everyday life of citizens.\n\nIn the conversation with Marić, Šarić defines the need for **healthy economic protectionism** through an analysis of the three fundamental market freedoms – the flow of goods, capital, and people:\n\n1. **Freedom of flow of goods and consumer informedness:** Domestic producers, who often offer significantly higher-quality products, can hardly compete in price with global corporations that operate by lower standards. Contrary to the naive libertarian assumption that a buyer on the free market always makes a rational decision, Šarić points out that the average citizen, when buying a tomato that is 10 cents cheaper, does not have complete information about who reaps the profit, in what conditions it was produced, how much it was treated with pesticides, and what health risks it carries. The state must therefore support local production and ensure the informedness of citizens.\n2. **The capital market and real estate:** Šarić warns of the destructiveness of the practice in which foreign funds and corporations are enabled to buy entire residential neighborhoods in Zagreb or real estate across Croatia. While international players use real estate as a store of capital, prices skyrocket, and for young Croatian families solving the housing issue becomes unattainable. The state would have to ensure a certain level of privilege for its own citizens in that segment.\n3. **Free flow of people:** As the third and most problematic dimension of an unrestricted market, Šarić announces the issue of mass migrations and the import of labor.",

     "subtitle": "Economic justifications for importing foreign workers and the unsustainability of the pension system",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić explains how behind the moral arguments for importing labor hides state-market exploitation.",
     "content": "Opening the topic of demography and mass migrations, host **Marin Marić** points out how the import of foreign workers and obtaining citizenship will certainly be a heated topic at the next elections in Croatia, asking the guest what the fundamental national consensus around that issue should be. **Petar Šarić** notices an interesting paradox on the Croatian political scene: the roles of the left and the right are completely swapped in relation to classical economic definitions. While the right is skeptical toward an absolutely free market that massively imports migrants, the left appeals to morality and market needs to justify that import, which shows how much political ideologies have lost their fundamental orientation.\n\nAnalyzing the justifications for importing foreign population, Šarić emphasizes that the whole story boils down to the need for cheap labor that would enable local employers good business operations, and citizens cheaper services. Although such an approach is often sold in the public as a highly moral act by which foreigners are enabled a better life, in practice it is a mere attempt at **state-market exploitation** without genuine respect for human dignity. He especially reflects on the frequent thesis that the pension system will collapse if migrants do not save it.\n\n\"Well, what migrant comes to Croatia with the goal of saving our pension system which is unsustainable?\", Šarić asks himself, concluding that such moral arguments in economic migrations immediately fall flat because the only real motive is exclusively economic benefit. If one truly believed in a democratic society, the guest considers, a referendum would be called on the import of foreign population, whereby he believes that citizens would sooner choose abstinence from import than integration. Marić builds on this with an assessment that the majority of citizens, due to the perception of a labor shortage, would probably support a quota system, but would sharply oppose foreign workers receiving Croatian citizenship overnight.",

    {
     "subtitle": "The myth of labor shortage versus technological innovations and automation",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić, using the vivid example of digging a pit with spoons and an excavator, explains the problem of accumulating cheap labor.",
     "content": "Upon the host's question about the minimal consensus for acquiring citizenship, **Petar Šarić** separates the mere legal basis of citizenship from the deeper question: when does a person truly become a member of the Croatian lineage and an integrated member of society. Before entering into the concept of integration itself, Šarić deconstructs the entrenched myth of the \"objective need for labor\", calling it a socially conditioned and ideological term. To vividly explain the absurdity of solving economic problems by the mere accumulation of people, he cites the example of digging a pit ten meters deep.\n\nIf the pit is dug with teaspoons, the employer will need ten thousand diligent workers, yet the question arises why no one is smart enough to pay for an excavator that will do that job for a hundred times lower price and in an incomparably shorter time. In practice, this means that employers would have to be more oriented toward **innovations** and rational organization of enterprises, because the objective need for labor is actually equal to the amount of problems that have not been solved by technology. In doing so, Šarić points to a huge contradiction in the public space:\n\n- On the one hand, the media daily bombard the public with news about **artificial intelligence** and automation because of which everyone will lose their jobs.\n- On the other hand, in parallel it is claimed that there is a never greater and inexhaustible need for importing labor.\n\nFrom this it follows that behind the alleged need for workers actually hides the maintenance of an unsustainable pension system and the maximization of GDP. Šarić poses the key question of whether those economic indicators are good enough that the fate of the Croatian people should be sacrificed for them. **Marin Marić** agrees with this thesis, warning that technological progress is inevitable and that automation in the long run will always be cheaper than cheap labor, which opens a serious question of what will happen with so much accumulated foreign labor at the moment when its work is no longer needed.",

     "subtitle": "A sociological view on the concept of integration and the responsibility of political elites",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić from a sociological perspective speaks about the non-existence of consensus around the concept of integration.",
     "content": "Reflecting on the concept of **integration**, which political elites often use as a magic word that provides citizens with an illusion of security, **Petar Šarić**, from the perspective of sociology, reveals how actually no one has any idea when someone is truly integrated. There is no scientific or social consensus on whether integration happens at the moment when a foreigner learns the language, when they start cheering for the national football team, or when they forget their mother tongue. Historically viewed, Šarić points out, different peoples successfully connected and achieved real coexistence almost exclusively in rare situations when they were faced with a common external threat in wars, which today is by no means an environment anyone would wish for.\n\nAnalyzing the approach of the right toward migrants, Šarić warns of the mistake when foreign workers are viewed as a malicious entity that came with the intention of conflict or spreading Sharia law, which can be only an eventual generational consequence. The vast majority of these people come out of mere materialistic motives – in order to earn money for their family or ensure a better education for their children. Therefore, the blame is not on the people who follow a material instinct, but on the **political elites** who opened the doors to mass migrations, consciously ignoring well-known negative consequences such as ghettoization, conflicts with the domestic population, and the loss of general security.\n\n**Marin Marić** proposes a possible political consensus that combines sustainable development through automation and respect for the dignity of the human person through stricter **labor rights**. If foreign workers were legally ensured equal working conditions, wages, and dignified accommodation such as domestic workers have, Marić considers that they would become less profitable to employers, whereby their import would be drastically reduced. Šarić evaluates this idea as an exceptionally interesting and realistic possibility worth thinking about more deeply.",

     "subtitle": "Transcendental human dignity as a condition for human rights",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić explains the philosophical difference between human dignity and international conventions on human rights.",
     "content": "Deepening the discussion on **human dignity** as a possible point of contact of political opposites, **Petar Šarić** defines the fundamental philosophical difference between the left and right currents. The right perspective is more willing to acknowledge that human dignity is transcendentally conditioned, that is, God-given, and that the value of man has a foundation that surpasses any worldly or state power. On the other hand, the left perspective gives primacy to the concept of **human rights**, which represent a material international convention.\n\nŠarić emphasizes how the key political question is what has primacy in that relationship. According to his opinion, the only sustainable thesis is that human dignity must be a prerequisite for human rights, and not the other way around. If man's value is reduced exclusively to rights guaranteed by the state or the international community, without transcendental dignity, then the most powerful global actors can by social convention at any moment completely erase, alter, or distort those rights.\n\nReturning that ontological perspective to the question of demography and foreign labor, Šarić concludes how the consensus must be built on the truth that the import of workers is no moral story at all, but pure exploitation for the sake of promised material benefit. In doing so, because of mild economic promises, such as GDP growth or paying taxes, the ethnic settings of the people itself are brought into question. If the average Croat were asked whether they want mild GDP growth or the preservation of the safety of their streets and the future of their children, Šarić is convinced that citizens would always choose safety, because of which society must focus on innovations instead of exhausting people from the Third World.",

     "subtitle": "Security consensus, investment in the military, and local energy self-sustainability",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić speaks about the decline of the unipolar world and the necessity of investing in the military and domestic production.",
     "content": "Moving on to the topic of national security, **Marin Marić** opens the question of determining a minimal consensus around the military and police. **Petar Šarić** points out how security is based on long-term rationality: a state cannot be stable if it continuously makes decisions that threaten that security, whether by uncontrolled import of labor, or by neglecting defense capacities. Given that the unipolarity of the world is declining, and with it global geopolitical security, it is common sense to invest in the military in order to preserve the existing way of life.\n\nIn doing so, Šarić points to a double paradox in the action of the green left:\n- Although the left greatly profits from the current Western order that legitimizes their decades-old ideas, at the moment when that order experiences challenges from **Russia** or **China**, they obstruct investments in the military that should defend that order.\n- Simultaneously, for moral reasons they advocate the uncontrolled import of migrants whose cultural values are in radical opposition to the ideology of the green left, not realizing that by doing so they are importing direct antagonists of their own worldview.\n\nWhile Marić concludes how methods like mandatory military service can be a subject of debate, but investment in defense itself must be unquestionable, Šarić expands the concept of security to **local production and energy sustainability**. Croatia currently achieves huge profit from tourism, yet the key question is whether that money is being invested in long-term survival, for instance in the development of **nuclear energy**. Speaking very realistically about demography, Šarić poses a strategic question: what if there are two million fewer Croats in forty years? In order for a smaller people to survive in such circumstances, it must ensure three key pillars: its own production of energy, a stable and equipped military, and local production of goods.",

     "subtitle": "Geopolitical positioning of Croatia between the weaknesses of the West and Eastern alternatives",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić analyzes the advantages and weaknesses of Western integrations in relation to Russia and China.",
     "content": "In the context of the creation of a multipolar world, **Marin Marić** notices increasingly present Eastern influences in the political space and asks whether the consensus on Croatia as a Western state needs to be brought to awareness again. **Petar Šarić** advocates for a sober approach that will not close its eyes to the obvious weaknesses of the West and the **European Union**, where decadent and destructive ideologies are continuously pushed, and urban areas pay a high price for uncontrolled migrations. However, after those weaknesses are brought to awareness, it is necessary to recognize the positive sides as well: citizens within the Atlantic-Western and **NATO** framework have by far the best quality of life in the world, and that space represents the logical continuity of the Europe that Croats defended for centuries.\n\nŠarić explains how sympathizers of Russian or Chinese influence notice Western decadence very well, but due to cheap contrarianism they become blind to the positive aspects of the West, romanticizing Eastern alternatives in the process. He warns how **Russia** is by no means a promised traditional society, but a state with high rates of abortion and marriage divorces, which until thirty years ago was part of the socialist **USSR**, from whose framework today's political elites also emerged.\n\nCroatia must therefore remain in the West which provides it with the protection of sovereignty, and membership in the European Union gives it objective international prestige – which Šarić illustrates with the example of a Croatian citizen behind whom in some African country stands the entire Union, unlike a citizen of **Montenegro**. Nevertheless, instead of blind obedience such as domestic elites often practice just to be invited to the table in the **European Commission**, Croatia must retain a backbone, autonomy, and the courage to sometimes say \"no\" at that table.",

     "subtitle": "The historical role of Croatia as the bulwark of Christianity and a cure for contemporary Europe",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić passionately speaks about Croatia as a historical and crucial country that must take the lead in Europe.",
     "content": "Building on the concept of political backbone, **Marin Marić** points out how belonging to Europe must not be viewed through a shallow financial transaction of what we received or lost, nor through Third-World narratives about Europe and the white man as a universal evil.
